Some uncertainty remains about the exact route of the Strada del Cifalco, as it developed historically.

Firstly, as is well known, old topographic maps abound with errors. This is particularly true up to the 1700s. Our Road is no exception to this observation.

Secondly, the routes had many variants: this is true of all the Salt Roads. Indeed, the succession of the seasons could entail some adjustment to the original route as proposed here, particularly for weather reasons: for example, to avoid snow on the slopes less exposed to the sun in winter, or, on the contrary, to seek coolness in summer, and so on. But that is not all. Solidarity among muleteers was such that sightings of bandits were promptly passed on, as they went, to those coming from the opposite direction, prompting them to change course. To this were added practical matters, since the passage of cows heading to or returning from the pastures next to the ridge could block the narrow paths, considerably slowing the muleteers’ progress.

Thirdly and lastly, while those arriving from the sea generally joined the Strada del Cifalco at Barbagelata, the route to follow up to that point was not a single one, but depended on the seaside town the muleteers set out from (Genoa, Sori, Portofino, Camogli, Rapallo and so on). The same applied to those coming from the plain. In short, at Barbagelata the route underwent a structural branching.

Note that, at the time, the muleteers completed the journey, in principle, in three days and two nights. The latter were often spent, respectively, on the meadows of Monte Dego and at Barbagelata. Then as now, places to eat along the Way were scarce and, for those with more elaborate itineraries in mind, it was essential to go down to eat and sleep in the villages in the valleys on one of the two sides. This phenomenon acted as a further factor in the proliferation of exits, detours and variants.

The route proposed here therefore combines philological rigour with the spectacular nature of the itinerary. It offers a base track from Ponte Organasco to Portofino Mare and points out the main (and most interesting) variants and detours, where appropriate.

The main Way thus climbs from Ponte Organasco to Cerignale, and then to Oneto and the summit of Monte delle Tane among oaks, hazels and hornbeams, along an ascent that is not very steep but steady. From here, it stays on the Trebbia-Aveto ridge as far as Barbagelata, passing beside the summits of the most representative mountains of the walk: Veri, Dego, Oramara, Montarlone, Roccabruna, Gifarco. These can be tackled by leaving the main Way for more or less short detours. From Barbagelata, it descends briefly to the Passo della Scoglina, then climbs again (and here, yes, rather steeply!) to the summit of M. Caucaso.

Following the watershed towards the sea westwards, it descends into the Val Fontanabuona through the little valley of the Neirone stream, as far as Gattorna; from here, having crossed the Lavagna stream, it climbs resolutely to the Passo dei Casetti, where a traverse opens up with views over the “two gulfs” (Tigullio and Paradiso) as far as Ruta and then through the Parco del M. di Portofino.

In keeping with the historical “fan-shaped” layout of the route, it is possible to end the walk differently, descending to the sea at Recco, Camogli, San Fruttuoso and Santa Margherita Ligure, depending on the point at which one leaves the main line.
